# Issues found in the synthetic intakes

**Status: all three resolved.** A corrected set was generated by Gemini 3.1 Pro and
is now in `eval/intakes`. Gold labelling is no longer blocked.

These intakes were generated by Gemini 3.1 Pro. The problems below were found after
the first generation and were not fixed in place, because correcting them by hand in a
different model would have defeated the reason a different model wrote them. They were
sent back to Gemini instead, and the record of what was wrong is kept here.

Both the original and the corrected files validate cleanly against intake schema
1.2.0. Every issue below is a content problem that the schema cannot catch, which is
the part worth remembering: a schema checks shape, not sense. Three defects survived
validation, and what caught them was a person reading the files.

This file lives in `docs/` rather than beside the intakes, and says nothing about how
any of this would be scored, so that it can be read at any point without affecting a
labelling pass. See the note at the end.

## 1. Weekly time figures on processes that do not run weekly. Resolved

`hours_per_week` only means anything for a process that runs every week. Where it was
given for an occasional process, multiplying it out over a 48 week working year
produced an annual total far larger than the description supported.

All three now use `minutes_per_case`, sized so the annual total matches what the
description says happens.

| File | Process | Frequency | Was | Annual equivalent | Now | Annual equivalent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| corner-pharmacy | `inventory-audit` | quarterly | 15 hours a week | 720 hours a year | 960 minutes per case | 64 hours a year |
| corner-pharmacy | `tax-preparation` | annually | 2 hours a week | 96 hours a year | 1440 minutes per case | 24 hours a year |
| bean-and-bark-roasters | `equipment-calibration` | annually | 0.5 hours a week | 24 hours a year | 120 minutes per case | 2 hours a year |

## 2. A time figure that contradicted its own pain text. Resolved

| File | Process | Was | Annual equivalent | Now | Annual equivalent | Pain text describes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| boutique-landscaping | `material-sourcing` | 15 hours a week | 720 hours a year | 4 hours a week | 192 hours a year | wasting a Thursday morning |

The number and the prose now agree. A Thursday morning is about four hours, and the
field says four hours a week.

## 3. data_notes present on one process out of fifteen. Resolved

Only `green-intake` in bean-and-bark-roasters carried a `data_notes` field. The field
is optional, so this passed validation, but fourteen processes silent on where their
data lives was a gap rather than a realistic spread.

All fifteen processes now have `data_notes`, five in each file.

## What this leaves for next time

Nothing here was caught by the schema, and nothing here would have been caught by a
stricter one without asking for fields a business owner cannot answer. Two of the
three were a stated figure disagreeing with the prose beside it, which is a check a
person can make in seconds and a validator cannot make at all.

That is worth carrying into the intake chatbot when it is built. A conversation can
ask why a quarterly task takes fifteen hours every week. A form cannot.

## What this file deliberately leaves out

Nothing here says what any of these processes would score, which criterion each field
feeds, or which direction an error would push a result. That is not an oversight.

Gold labels are written blind, and a labeller who has read that a particular process
would score high or low on a particular criterion is no longer labelling blind. The
value of the whole exercise depends on the labels being one person's independent
judgement, so a defects list has to be readable without contaminating it.

Nor is anything here a judgement about whether the businesses are plausible or whether
the processes are good automation candidates. Those are the questions the gold labels
exist to answer, and pre judging them in this file would contaminate the labelling in
exactly the same way.
